title: 2025 budget direction and grants policy changes
subtitle: Reserve use, service reduction rankings, in-year budget requests, police staffing cost request and budget amendment deadlines also considered.
overview: The Strategic Planning and Budget Committee met to set the stage for the 2025 Plan and Budget. Staff said the current draft shows a property tax increase of 12.1% with service expansions, and about 9 to 10% for the base budget alone. Council's guideline is under 8%, which staff said would require reducing or eliminating some services. All figures are draft, and the preliminary budget is due on October 30.

The committee recommended that Council adopt most of the recommendations from its summer sub-committee. These include changing how grants are approved, testing cost assumptions such as fuel, looking at more use of the tax stabilization reserve, speeding up the Provincial Offences Act expansion, and requiring staff to rank service reduction options by risk. It also recommended that new in-year spending requests go to the budget process and show two-year tax impacts. One recommendation, on deferring service expansions, was held back until staff present them.

The committee also recommended a notice deadline of December 2, 2024 for budget amendment motions, to be used in future years. A request to waive notice for a police staffing cost motion was defeated {{vote:m14}}. Closed session was held on labour relations and personal matters; the minutes report no public outcome.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that Council approve grant streams and eligibility while staff administer grants, review the policy in the second year of each term, create new grants only as new streams through the budget process, and require applicants to declare other municipal grants {{vote:m1}}.
The committee directed staff to review and revise budget cost assumptions, including fuel and other variable costs, to take on more risk {{vote:m3}}.
The committee directed staff to explore using the tax stabilization reserve further to reduce the tax burden of one-time expenditures {{vote:m4}}.
The committee directed staff to action the POA expansion immediately as a 2024 in-year request to maximize 2025 revenue {{vote:m5}}.
The committee directed staff to present a ranked list of service reduction options with low, medium and high risk ratings {{vote:m6}}.
The committee recommended that any new net budget increase requests made during the year be deferred to the Strategic Planning and Budget process {{vote:m8}}.
The committee directed staff to ensure Council budget increase requests include projected tax impacts for the next two years {{vote:m7}}.

The committee amended and adopted a rule that motions to amend the final budget must be submitted in writing by Monday, December 2, 2024, with the process also applying to future budgets {{vote:m13}}.

debate: On the grants policy, supporters said it would cut one-off in-year approvals that raise future levies, give community groups clear timelines, and make funding more transparent. Critics said it was beyond the sub-committee's purpose of reducing the tax increase, needed a staff report first, and could leave some communities, such as Cambridge, underfunded. A deferral to March 2025 was defeated {{vote:m2}}.

On the tax stabilization reserve, one councillor asked what guardrails applied. Staff said it holds a $13.9 million opening balance with about $10 million already committed, and that it suits one-time or phased-in costs, not ongoing ones. Another councillor warned that using it for tax relief would remove one of the few safety nets.

On ranking service reductions, some councillors called it redundant or vague, and worried about effects on townships and vulnerable groups. Staff said they would use the existing Council risk matrix, which covers reputational, financial, litigation and staffing risks. Several councillors asked that social risks and longer-term benefits also be reported.

On deferring in-year requests, opponents said it limits Council's flexibility when urgent needs arise. Supporters said in-year approvals have added millions to later budgets and favour groups that know how to lobby, and that a clear process is fairer.

On fuel assumptions, staff explained that taking more risk means budgeting a lower fuel price. They noted the 2024 budget assumed $1.50 per litre against an average closer to $1.36. A councillor asked for a paper explaining the approach.
